Sophocles in Nauplius Pyrcaeus: “they hang down below, a σπίζα stretched out in the enclosures.” ἄζα, γάζα, and Γάζα, a city of Phoenicia, but now of Palestine, before Egypt. It was also called Ἄζα. And even to this day the Syrians call it Ἄζα, from Ἄζων, the son of Heracles. Some relate in myth that it was founded by Zeus and that in it he left his own γάζα, since thus the Persians call money. μύζα, κνύζα, which, if it is said of the plant, is a syncope, as in “of the lowly κονύζη”; but if it is said of what is corrupted and filthy, it is not a syncope, but from κνύω, from which comes κνύος, “decay,” as in “he poured it forth in decay, and the heads were stripped bare”; and thus κνύζα is formed, as in Anacreon: “I am already becoming some κνύζη and worn out through your madness” (fr. 87 Bergk). δόξα. Φρίξα, a city of Triphylia, from Phrixus, on a high mountain toward the east of the Lepreatis. Pherecydes, however, writes it as belonging to Arcadia. Λίξα, a city of Libya, as Alexander says in the first book of the Libyca, from the river Λίξος. δίψα. Κάψα, a city of the Chalcidic region in Pallene, bordering on the Thermaic Gulf. Σάμψα, a village of Arabia; and among the Arabs σάμψα is the sun. Σκέμψα, a city of Thrace. Στρέψα, a city of Macedonia. Hecataeus in the Circuit of Asia: “and the lake has the name Δούριζα.” Βόρυζα, a Persian city, as Hecataeus in the Circuit of Europe: “and after that, Βόρυζα, a city of the Persians; and after that, Thynias.” Ἀράβυζα, a city of Cauconis. Τὰ δὲ ὑπερδισύλλαβα προπαροξύνεται, ὄρυζα, τράπεζα· ἔστι καὶ πόλις Ἀρκαδίας ἐγγὺς Τρικολώνων. ἀργυρόπεζα, τετράπεζα, χάλαζα, Δούριζα λίμνη παρὰ τὸν Λίζαν ποταμόν. Βάδιζα πόλις Βρεττίας. Πολύβιος τρισκαιδεκάτῳ. Βαρύγαζα ἐμπόριον Γεδρωσίας τῶν σφόδρα ἐπισήμων. Μίεζα θυγάτηρ Βέρητος τοῦ Μακεδόνος καὶ πόλις Μακεδονίας. Κάττουζα πόλις Θρᾴκης, ἐν ᾗ κατῴκουν οἱ Πυγμαῖοι. Θελάμουζα φρούριον τῆς παρ´ Εὐφράτην Ἀραβίας. Τίριζα πόλις Παφλαγονίας. Τυρόδιζα πόλις Θρᾴκης μετὰ Σέρριον. Ἑλλάνικος δὲ Τυρόριζαν αὐτήν φησιν ἐν Περσικῶν δευτέρῳ. ἅμαξα. Ἄμαξα χωρίον Βιθυνίας, ὡς Ἐρατοσθένης. Ἄραξα πόλις Λυκίας, ὡς Ἀλέξανδρος ἐν δευτέρῳ τῶν Λυκιακῶν. Δάραψα πόλις Βακτρίας, ὡς Στράβων. Herodian’s Accent Toy: -αιος / -αυος / -οιος (disyllables)

Type a Greek word (or make one up). The toy guesses whether it matches Herodian’s patterns and suggests an accent (acute vs “grave”/circumflex-style). It’s a playful helper, not a full accent engine.

Result

—
Enter a word to see a suggested accent and rule.

How it plays (from the passage)

  • -αιος disyllables (not proper names) → acute (e.g. λαιός, φαιός, βαιός, σκαιός).
  • -αυος disyllables → “grave”/recessive-looking (e.g. ναῦος, αὗος). (Toy uses a circumflex on the first vowel.)
  • -οιος disyllables → acute, except interrog./relative-like forms (ποῖος, τοῖος, κοῖος, οἷος) → “grave”/recessive-looking.

Tip: you can type without accents (λαιος) or with them (λαιός). The toy will normalize and re-accent.

Accent sandbox

Toggle what kind of word you intend (Herodian’s exceptions depend on this).

This is just for play: it swaps endings and re-accents using the same toy rules.

What the toy is (and isn’t)

This gadget focuses on a narrow slice of Herodian’s discussion: accent tendencies for disyllables in -αιος, -αυος, -οιος, plus a small exception list (ποῖος, τοῖος, κοῖος, οἷος) and a “proper name” toggle. It does not compute full Greek accentuation, vowel quantity, enclitics, or real prosodic rules beyond these patterns.

original.english_translation: “the springs of the Ister.” And among the Attic writers too the names of household slaves are Δᾶοι and Γέται; and Δᾶκος is also said. Further, there is also a river Λᾶος and a city of Lucania, as Apollodorus says in the second book of his On the Earth; and Λᾶοι are those who inhabit Λᾶν, a city of Laconia. Χνᾶος is an ethnicon. And πρᾷος too is an epithet. But among the Alexandrians ταός is noted as used in place of ταὧς. And the λᾶος in Sophocles, “upon the edge of the λάος” (Oed. Col. 195), has been changed into the nominative from the genitive λᾶος in “λᾶος under a gust” (Μ 462). Disyllables in -αιος, if they are not proper names, are accented with an acute: λαιός, φαιός, βαιός, σκαιός the epithet. But Σκαῖος is the proper name, as also Βαῖος, the helmsman of Odysseus, and Γραῖος, Παῖος. Disyllables in -αυος are accented with a grave: ναῦος, αὗος ‘the dry.’ Αὖος is a river of Thesprotia; Τραῦος is a proper name, and also Ψαῦος in Alcman. But ἀγαυός is trisyllabic. Disyllables in -οιος are accented with an acute, unless they are proper names or interrogative or relative forms and the initial ο is an addition: σμοιός an epithet, σκλοιός for σκολιός, δοιός, γλοιός of dung, βοιός, κλοιός, which is also said as κλῳός, φλοιός. But ποῖος, τοῖος, κοῖος, οἷος are accented with a grave.

Accent patterns in -αιος, -αυος and -οιος

Try a Greek word to see how the disyllable patterns in Herodian 1.109 apply.

Result

Enter a word to see a suggested accent and rule.

Rules in the passage

  • -αιος disyllables take an acute on the final syllable in common words such as σκαιός. The proper name Σκαῖος takes a circumflex.
  • Herodian describes disyllables in -αυος as βαρύνεται. His examples ναῦος and αὗος have a circumflex on the first syllable.
  • -οιος disyllables such as κλοιός take an acute on the final syllable under the usual rule. In describing the exceptions, Herodian mentions proper names, interrogative and relative forms, and an added initial ο. The passage lists ποῖος, τοῖος, κοῖος, οἷος with circumflexes.

original.english_translation: “the springs of the Ister.” And among the Attic writers too the names of household slaves are Δᾶοι and Γέται; and Δᾶκος is also said. Further, there is also a river Λᾶος and a city of Lucania, as Apollodorus says in the second book of his On the Earth; and Λᾶοι are those who inhabit Λᾶν, a city of Laconia. Χνᾶος is an ethnicon. And πρᾷος too is an epithet. But among the Alexandrians ταός is noted as used in place of ταὧς. And the λᾶος in Sophocles, “upon the edge of the λάος” (Oed. Col. 195), has been changed into the nominative from the genitive λᾶος in “λᾶος under a gust” (Μ 462). Disyllables in -αιος, if they are not proper names, are accented with an acute: λαιός, φαιός, βαιός, σκαιός the epithet. But Σκαῖος is the proper name, as also Βαῖος, the helmsman of Odysseus, and Γραῖος, Παῖος. Disyllables in -αυος are accented with a grave: ναῦος, αὗος ‘the dry.’ Αὖος is a river of Thesprotia; Τραῦος is a proper name, and also Ψαῦος in Alcman. But ἀγαυός is trisyllabic. Disyllables in -οιος are accented with an acute, unless they are proper names or interrogative or relative forms and the initial ο is an addition: σμοιός an epithet, σκλοιός for σκολιός, δοιός, γλοιός of dung, βοιός, κλοιός, which is also said as κλῳός, φλοιός. But ποῖος, τοῖος, κοῖος, οἷος are accented with a grave.
original.gadget_html:
Herodian’s Accent Toy: -αιος / -αυος / -οιος (disyllables)

Type a Greek word (or make one up). The toy guesses whether it matches Herodian’s patterns and suggests an accent (acute vs “grave”/circumflex-style). It’s a playful helper, not a full accent engine.

Result

—
Enter a word to see a suggested accent and rule.

How it plays (from the passage)

  • -αιος disyllables (not proper names) → acute (e.g. λαιός, φαιός, βαιός, σκαιός).
  • -αυος disyllables → “grave”/recessive-looking (e.g. ναῦος, αὗος). (Toy uses a circumflex on the first vowel.)
  • -οιος disyllables → acute, except interrog./relative-like forms (ποῖος, τοῖος, κοῖος, οἷος) → “grave”/recessive-looking.

Tip: you can type without accents (λαιος) or with them (λαιός). The toy will normalize and re-accent.

This is just for play: it swaps endings and re-accents using the same toy rules.

What the toy is (and isn’t)

This gadget focuses on a narrow slice of Herodian’s discussion: accent tendencies for disyllables in -αιος, -αυος, -οιος, plus a small exception list (ποῖος, τοῖος, κοῖος, οἷος) and a “proper name” toggle. It does not compute full Greek accentuation, vowel quantity, enclitics, or real prosodic rules beyond these patterns.
